title: Scalable methylome-transcriptome profiling resolves clonal organization in human hematopoiesis
authors: Shao, J.; Chen, M.; Liu, Y.; Sun, J.; Zhang, G.; Yan, Z.-Y.; Lin, H.; Ren, M.; Pei, S.; Peng, J.; Gong, Y.; Wang, S.-W.
abstract: Understanding human tissue maintenance and remodeling requires linking clonal ancestry to molecular state, yet scalable joint measurement remains challenging. Here, we introduce Droplet-MT and an integrated computational workflow for joint transcriptome and methylome profiling at ~10,000 cells per library. Methylation epimutations enable mutation-independent clonal reconstruction from high-coverage methylomes, while reference-based label transfer assigns cells to established clones at ~0.2% CpG coverage, reducing sequencing cost. Clone-aggregated somatic variants provide genetic annotation without additional single-cell genotyping. Across ~21,000 paired profiles from healthy blood and longitudinal acute myeloid leukemia, we resolved small and expanded clones with heterogeneous lineage output. In leukemia, the framework distinguished changes in malignant clonal abundance, state remodeling within persistent clones, and recovery of healthy polyclonal hematopoiesis. Malignant monocytes remained transcriptionally and epigenetically distinct from healthy and recovery-associated cells despite treatment-associated remodeling. Droplet-MT enables scalable analysis of human tissues by linking clonal organization with molecular state and retrospective genetic annotation.

title: Aggregate Deep Visual Proteomics reveals selective organization of α-synuclein inclusions
authors: Oeller, M.; Vasconez Grunauer, S.; Sitron, C. S.; Mahul Mellier, A.-L.; Diedrich, L.; Schuele, A.; Ruf, V.; Oliinyk, D.; Kuttler, F.; Dransfeld, U.; Prassler, J.; Ben-Moshe, S.; Rodriguez, E.; Heymann, T.; Ugur, E.; Madden, K.; Sun, Y.; Ulrich, C.; Jasiqi, Y.; Lashuel, H. A.; Hartl, F. U.; Mann, M.
abstract: -Synuclein inclusions, the lesions typical of Parkinson's disease, have been interpreted as protective deposits, toxic species or failed degradation products, each predicting a different composition and correlating that enrichment with neuron dysfunction and eventual degeneration. Distinguishing them requires measuring what an inclusion concentrates relative to the cell that built it. Here we developed Aggregate Deep Visual Proteomics, which uses ultrasensitive mass spectrometry to profile laser-microdissected inclusions against the remainder of the same cell or a matched host. In HEK293 cells, iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons and post-mortem patient brain, each inclusion concentrated a selective subset of its cell's proteome, independent of abundance and dominated by membrane, in neurons largely presynaptic. Inclusions took up whole assemblies, with subunits moving together in 421 of 438 complexes, and the V-ATPase alone was enriched in all three systems. Degradation cargo stayed with the receptors that route it, consistent with sequestration and failed degradation acting together. Neuritic and somatic inclusions differed, the former rich in UBQLN2 and the latter in intermediate filaments. In the cell line, phosphorylated -synuclein was tenfold higher in the inclusion than in the rest of the cell, with about one third of the rise already present before an inclusion was visible. Measured against its host, the composition of an inclusion becomes a readout of how it formed and a source of candidate markers and therapeutic targets.

title: Clinical-Anchored Incremental Survival Learning: A Stability-Constrained Framework for Molecularly Enhanced Survival Prediction in Lung Adenocarcinoma
authors: Shringarpure, P.; Divakar, S.; Khobragade, S.
abstract: Accurate survival prediction in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remains challenging because high-dimensional molecular data can introduce overfitting and unstable feature selection. We developed Clinical-Anchored Incremental Survival Learning (CAISL), a framework that integrates a sparse molecular risk correction with a clinical baseline to improve prognostic discrimination while constraining model complexity and prediction variability. CAISL was evaluated using The Cancer Genome Atlas LUAD cohort comprising 470 patients and 119 observed deaths. Performance was compared with clinical Cox, molecular-only, and unanchored multimodal models using five independently seeded, event-stratified five-fold cross-validation runs. CAISL achieved a mean concordance index (C-index) of 0.7246, compared with 0.6970 for clinical Cox, yielding an absolute improvement of 0.0276 (95% bootstrap confidence interval [CI], 0.005 to 0.050). Time-dependent discrimination was higher at three years (AUC, 0.742 vs. 0.712) and five years (AUC, 0.721 vs. 0.691), while the integrated Brier score was lower for CAISL than for clinical Cox (0.164 vs. 0.181). Ablation analysis identified clinical anchoring as the component associated with the largest reduction in discrimination when removed. Stability analysis showed a mean pairwise Jaccard similarity of 0.46 between selected feature sets and a mean Spearman correlation of 0.86 between molecular correction scores. These findings support the potential of clinically anchored, stability-constrained molecular learning to improve internal survival-risk prediction in LUAD. Independent-cohort validation is needed to establish generalizability.

title: Amide I kurtosis maps cardiac amyloid in human tissue by ultrabroadband multiplex coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) microscopy
authors: Ota, K.; Chen, T.-H.; Yamaguchi, T.; Otsubo, T.; Murakami, Y.; Masaki, M.; Leproux, P.; Suzuki, R.; Node, K.; Kano, H.
abstract: Cardiac amyloidosis is caused by deposits of misfolded proteins in the heart and can lead to heart failure. Histological confirmation typically involves staining tissue sections with Congo red and examining them under polarized light for apple-green birefringence; however, achieving an interpretable, label-free, and observer-independent assessment remains challenging. Here we show that Pearson kurtosis of channel intensities within the amide I window provides an interpretable, fitting-free contrast for cardiac amyloid in unstained human cardiac tissue sections imaged by ultrabroadband multiplex coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS). In two participants, high-kurtosis regions corresponded with Congo red-positive tissue in adjacent stained sections (descriptive spatial AUCs, 0.79 and 0.73). Across 15 fields from nine participants, including one of these two, kurtosis values did not overlap between severe-deposition and amyloid-negative tissue. Among the descriptors examined, kurtosis showed the largest standardized participant-level separation. Exploratory multivariate curve resolution yielded a deposit-associated component with aromatic-residue features shared with reagent transthyretin. Second harmonic generation (SHG), acquired simultaneously with CARS, showed a broadly inverse spatial pattern relative to kurtosis, providing complementary architectural contrast. These findings support a label-free approach to detecting cardiac amyloid deposits that combines broadband CARS-derived amide I kurtosis with SHG.

title: Dissociating Resting-State Networks of Pedohebephilic Preference and Child Sexual Offending Using Network-Based Prediction
authors: Serin, E.; Khan, K. R.; Krueger, T.; Sinke, C.; Beier, K. M.; Walter, M.; Schiffer, B.; Amelung, T.; Walter, H.
abstract: Pedohebephilia (P+), the sexual preference for prepubescent and early pubertal minors, regularly causes distress in those affected. While associated with child sexual offending (CSO), P+ is not a prerequisite for CSO. Limited neuroimaging studies have identified alterations associated with P+, while these may primarily reflect offending history. The correlates of P+ independent of CSO therefore remain unclear. We examined this distinction using intrinsic functional networks within a multivariate predictive framework. Using resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) and network-based prediction (NBS-Predict), we performed pairwise classifications among non-offending pedohebephilic men (P+CSO-, n=35), pedohebephilic men with CSO (P+CSO+, n=38), and non-pedohebephilic controls without CSO (P-CSO-, n=63). Classification-relevant subnetwork nodal strength was associated post hoc with trait impulsivity within P+ groups. P+CSO- were significantly distinguished from P-CSO- (balanced accuracy [BAC]=.621, pFDR=.041), and showed reductions between default-mode hubs and temporoparietal somatomotor and ventral attention regions. P+CSO+ were also significantly distinguished from P+CSO- (BAC=.645, pFDR=.032) and yielded a smaller subnetwork centered on the substantia nigra. Against P-CSO-, P+CSO+ showed widespread reductions, particularly across subcortical, default mode, visual, limbic, and somatomotor regions (BAC=.640, pFDR=.032). Right precentral gyrus nodal strength correlated with impulsivity in P+CSO+ only (r = .57, pFDR=.024). Whole-brain rsFC contains information, distinguishing pedohebephilic preference in the absence of known CSO, while P+CSO+ show additional, more widespread network alterations involving systems implicated in action selection and behavioral regulation. These findings open new avenues for integrating pedohebephilia into broader neurobiological research frameworks.

title: Sex differences in cell type-specific transcriptional programs and GPCR signaling in the human subgenual anterior cingulate cortex
authors: Snowden, A. W.; Li, N. Y.; Sibille, E.; Joffe, M. E.; Seney, M. L.
abstract: Psychiatric conditions show marked sex differences in disease onset, symptom presentation, and response to treatments. Understanding how sex differences manifest across molecularly distinct neuronal populations in individuals without psychiatric conditions may help explain sex-dependent variation in neural circuit function and treatment response. Here, we examined molecularly distinct cell types within the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) of non-psychiatric subjects. Using RNA sequencing data previously generated from laser-capture microdissected neurons, we investigated sex differences in gene expression and co-expression networks in excitatory pyramidal neurons (layers 2/3 and 5/6) and somatostatin (SST)-, parvalbumin (PVALB)-, and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)-expressing inhibitory interneurons (N=10 males, 9 females). We identified sex differences in transcriptomic profiles, biological pathways, and co-expression network connectivity. PVALB cells showed stronger overall female transcriptional enrichment, while SST cells exhibited male-enriched transcriptional signatures. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis identified PVALB and SST modules more connected in males and females, respectively, which included hub genes involved in immune, extracellular matrix, and bioenergetic processes. Since G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are viable therapeutic targets, we examined sex differences in GPCR transcripts. Across all GPCR-cell-type combinations, CHRM2 in PVALB cells showed the second strongest sex difference (enriched in females). To test the functional relevance of this difference, we used patch-clamp electrophysiology in mouse prefrontal cortex. M2 receptor activation increased maximal firing rates in PVALB cells from female but not male mice. Collectively, our findings demonstrate cell type-specific sex differences in the sgACC corresponding to functional differences in neuromodulator signaling, with potential implications for treatment response.

title: Temporal stability for individual differences in both habit learning and expression
authors: Martinez-Lopez, P.; Leon, J. J.; Garre-Frutos, F.; Vazquez-Millan, A.; Molinero, S.; Gimenez-Fernandez, T.; Vadillo, M. A.; Luque, D.
abstract: Actions transition from goal-directed to stimulus-driven habits through repetition. Individual differences in the capacity to learn and control habits are central to current models of psychopathology, which assume that overreliance on habitual control drives maladaptive behaviors. However, whether these tendencies reflect stable, trait-like cognitive processes remains unclear. We examined the temporal stability of individual differences in habit learning and expression. Across two preregistered experiments (total N = 313), we assessed stimulus-response habits using the same stimuli after one day or different stimuli after four months. Evidence for stable individual differences in habit commissions was strong and comparable across experiments, with computational modelling further supporting trait-like tendencies for habit learning and expression. Trait-like tendencies were also reflected in action automatization while practicing stimulus-response associations, which was associated with future habitual behavior. Our findings have theoretical implications for our understanding of habit formation and its role in psychopathology.

title: The C. elegans Connectome Toolbox: an open, extensible framework for multimodal connectomic data integration and analysis
authors: Vickneswaran, Y.; Ponzi, A.; Sinha, A.; Cohen, N.; Larson, S.; Gleeson, P.
abstract: The nematode C. elegans is one of the best studied model organisms in biology. Since the initial description of the C. elegans neuronal connectome by White and colleagues, numerous studies have mapped and analyzed the connectome, and released structured datasets of the connectivity, often merging and adding to previous versions. These datasets now serve as foundational resources that underpin studies into the neuronal basis of C. elegans behavior. In spite of their high utility, heterogeneity in the different datasets and their annotation conventions obscures direct comparison where discrepancies between connectomes frequently stem from differences in coverage or nomenclature rather than genuine biological disagreement. Additionally, datasets describing new connectivity modalities - contact-based (the contactome), extrasynaptic (monoaminergic and neuropeptidergic), and functional connectivity - have also recently become available. Thus, there is a need for a unified framework providing standardized access to these diverse datasets while preserving their individual provenance. Here, we present the C. elegans Connectome Toolbox, a comprehensive framework for consolidating, curating and validating historical and newly published multimodal C. elegans connectivity data. Connectome Toolbox includes an accessible online resource (https://openworm.org/ConnectomeToolbox) for interactive data exploration and is accompanied by a Python library for programmatic access. We demonstrate the utility of the toolbox through a series of analyses that illustrate how connectome data can be explored, visualized, and compared across modalities, including integration of the anatomical connectome with a comprehensive neurotransmitter atlas, and comparison with computational models of C. elegans neural circuits.

title: 40 Hz visual stimulation increases gamma-band functional connectivity between visual, parietal and frontal regions
authors: Ma, T.; Sun, Q.; Mlinaric, T.; Van Hulle, M. M.
abstract: Visual stimulation at 40 Hz is being investigated as a non-invasive intervention for Alzheimer's disease. Its neural responses have been reported in regions beyond the visual cortex, and concurrent cognitive tasks have been shown to increase their spatial extent. However, it is unclear whether these responses reflect increased functional connectivity between regions or a common response to the stimulus, and whether a concurrent task changes this connectivity. We recorded EEG from 29 healthy young adults during Regular 40 Hz flicker and Irregular 30-50 Hz flicker, each with and without a target-counting task (2 x 2 within-participant design). Source-space connectivity between visual, parietal, and frontal regions was estimated with the debiased squared weighted phase-lag index (dWPLI). Regular stimulation increased 38-42 Hz connectivity for all three region pairs, with the largest increase between visual and parietal regions (increase in all 29 participants). The increase was specific to the stimulation frequency and was observed with two source reconstruction methods and in sensor space. The visual-parietal increase remained significant after correction for source leakage (spatial mixing between reconstructed sources) and after removal of the estimated stimulus-locked component, whereas the increases in visual-frontal and parietal-frontal connectivity did not. The concurrent task did not modulate the visual-parietal effect. For visual-frontal and parietal-frontal connectivity, the stimulation-by-ask interaction was not significant. These results show that 40 Hz visual stimulation increases gamma-band connectivity beyond the visual cortex, and much of this increase reflects a common stimulus-locked response, and connectivity beyond this response was observed mainly between visual and parietal regions.

title: Social vision expands into auditory cortices of people born deaf: evidence from naturalistic film and encoding models
authors: Zimmermann, M.; Szwed, M.; Isik, L.; Bedny, M.
abstract: Comparing deaf and hearing adults provides insight into the contribution of experience to function of auditory cortical networks. We used naturalistic fMRI and voxel-wise encoding to measure information processing in auditory networks of deaf (n=24) and hearing (n=22) adults who watched a 35-minute silent animated film. Unlike simpler stimuli, naturalistic films are rich in a broad range of perceptual, affective, and social features, including motion, dynamic social interactions, and Theory of Mind. Machine vision algorithms and human coding were used to densely annotate visual and social film features. In both groups we observed a right-lateralized processing hierarchy with encoding of low-level visual features in early visual areas, social visual features along the superior temporal sulcus (STS) and Theory of Mind in temporoparietal junction. In deaf participants, auditory cortices showed enhanced encoding of a broad range of visual information, from low level motion to Theory of Mind. In higher order auditory networks, social interactions emerging as the strongest predictor of neural activity in deaf people and showed the strongest enhancement in deafness. Auditory networks of deaf adults showed systematic anatomical organization within and across hemispheres. Within the right hemisphere, higher-order auditory regions neighboring the STS preferentially responded to social visual features whereas lower-level visual features were represented broadly across the auditory hierarchy. These results suggest that proximity and connectivity principles govern anatomical expansion of information encoding in sensory loss.

title: Increased activity without changes in coupling between somata and apical dendrites during visual mismatches
authors: Henley, T. M.; Tindall, J.; Pina, J. E.; Pogodin, R.; Caldejon, S.; Orlova, N.; Amaya, A.; Bawany, A.; Grasso, C.; Groblewski, P.; Ha, V.; Han, W.; Johnson, T.; Naidoo, R.; Nguyen, K.; Seid, S.; Suarez, L.; Swapp, J.; Waughman, X.; Wilkes, J.; Williford, A.; Young, A.; Lecoq, J. A.; Zylberberg, J.; Richards, B. A.
abstract: Leading theories of cortical function posit that sensory processing involves a comparison between top-down predictions and bottom-up sensory data. Tests of these theories have been hampered by experimental challenges related to simultaneously recording top-down and bottom-up signals in response to sensory stimuli that either do or do not match internally-generated predictions. Here, we conduct dual-plane 2-photon calcium imaging near-simultaneously from distal apical dendrites and somata of pyramidal neurons in each of 4 different regions of mouse visual cortex while the mice are presented with visual sequences that can either match or mismatch previously habituated visual stimuli. Specifically, we examine the responses in the distal apical dendrites and cell bodies of pyramidal neurons while mice view either movie clips that reverse unexpectedly or Gabor patch sequences that have orientations that do not match habituated patterns. We find that in response to unexpected reversals in natural movies, both the apical dendrites and somata show increased activity that decreases over repeated exposures, consistent with a prediction error response. However, we do not find any clear evidence for increased activity in response to mismatches in Gabor sequences, beyond possible release from adaptation effects. We additionally use volumetric images to connect dendritic and somatic compartments and examine the coupling between connected dendrites and cell bodies in layer 5 pyramidal neurons. We do not find evidence for changes in coupling in response to mismatch stimuli, either for natural movies or Gabor sequences. Our results are consistent across four regions of visual cortex. We also observe that increased responses to reversals in natural movies are stronger in layer 2/3 than layer 5 pyramidal neurons. Altogether, these data suggest that visual cortex is sensitive to deviations from previously-experienced naturalistic inputs. Our data do not suggest that this mismatch sensitivity extends to artificial stimuli, nor do they support theories of prediction error causing changes in the coupling between apical dendrites and somata.

title: Optimal compositions of potent sliced-siRNA with DNA bases substitution and insights of Ago2 slicing actions
authors: Sun, G.; Lizhar, E. M.; Shi, Y.; Riggs, A. D.
abstract: We have previously characterized the nucleotide compositions of single-stranded ago2-sliced small interfering RNAs (sliced-siRNA, sliRNA), a novel type of potent RNAi trigger designed based on the biogenesis mechanism of miRNA-451. sliRNAs have on par antisense mediated silencing activity but about 1000-fold reduced passenger strand activity compared to siRNA. In the current study, to further characterize sliRNAs to facilitate their in vivo application, we have investigated the effects of substituting RNA nucleotides (nts) in sliRNA with DNA nts (sliDRNAs), which will allow us to study the potential effects on their processing, maturation, and silencing activity from individual or multiple nts at different positions. Our results showed sliDRNAs have distinguished composition from siRNA with DNA nts (siDRNA), indicated that, in addition to their different biogenesis mechanisms, these two types of RNAi triggers may also have adopted additional different silencing mechanisms. Our results also revealed some mechanism related to how Ago2 executes its slicer activity and the effects on sliRNA potency by trimming and tailing during sliRNA maturation. These results have paved the way for using other chemically modified nts in sliRNAs that may enhance their in vivo stability and transportability to facilitate their in vivo applications.

title: Insulin stimulation induces dynamic interaction between 14-3-3 and the C-terminal tail domain of Kinesin-2 subunit KIF3B in vitro
authors: Kumari, D.; Tangri, A.; Girotra, M.; Ray, K.
abstract: Heterotrimeric kinesin[ndash]2 mediates diverse intracellular transport processes, yet the mechanisms governing its cargo specificity and regulation remain poorly understood. In this study, we report the regulation of interaction between the kinesin[ndash]2 subunit KIF3B and a candidate adaptor protein, 14[ndash]3[ndash]3[epsilon];. Using splitAPEX2 proximity labelling and fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) assays in HEK293T cells, we demonstrate that 14[ndash]3[ndash]3[epsilon]; interacts with KIF3B within discrete subcellular compartments. This interaction is significantly enhanced upon insulin stimulation, indicating regulation by signalling pathways. Time resolved FLIM analysis further reveals that the site of interaction is dynamic, suggesting spatial and temporal control of motora[ndash]daptor association. Finally, the interactions are mapped to two serine residues in the C[ndash]terminal tail region of KIF3B that are highly conserved across species. Together, these findings uncover a conditional and reversible interaction between KIF3B and 14[ndash]3[ndash]3[epsilon], providing insight into how kinesin[ndash]2 may achieve context specific cargo engagement and transport within cells.

title: N-terminal cysteine independent effects of oxidative stress on the stability of RGS4 and 5
authors: Kim, H.; Shang, N.; Tian, Y.-M.; Ratcliffe, P.; Keeley, T. P.
abstract: Oxidative post-translational modifications on the sulfhydryl group of cysteines can occur spontaneously or enzymatically. The enzymatic dioxygenation of N-terminal cysteines has emerged as a new oxygen sensing paradigm, catalysed by 2-aminoethanethiol dioxygenase (ADO) in mammals. Conflicting evidence has been reported in recent years on whether this reaction can occur spontaneously in the absence of ADO. Here we sought to address whether cellular oxidative stress can interfere with ADO-catalysed N-terminal cysteine dioxygenation. Using a system to produce titratable intracellular levels of H2O2, we demonstrate that the stability of RGS4 and 5 is not affected by physiological levels of oxidative stress, whether ADO is present or not. However, cytotoxic levels of oxidative stress induced by tert-butyl hydroperoxide did induce a substantial increase in RGS4/5 protein stability that occurred independently of the Cys N-degron pathway. This effect of tBHP was abolished by Fe2+ chelation, lysosomal pH perturbation, and lipid peroxide scavenging. We conclude that N-terminal cysteine dependent proteolysis of RGS4/5 is not sensitive to physiological oxidative stress, but these proteins can be stabilised during the process of oxidative stress-induced cell death through an N-terminal cysteine independent mechanism.

title: Short-read whole-genome sequencing identifies the Tg(Tal1-cre/ERT)42-056Jrg transgene insertion site on mouse chromosome 4
authors: Wu, X.; Bagish, M. C.; Sanchez Vela, P.; Goglia, A. G.; Levine, R. L.
abstract: Tg(Tal1-cre/ERT)42-056Jrg, also known as HSC-Scl-CreERT, is a well-used transgenic allele that enables genetic manipulation in mouse hematopoietic cells. Using short-read whole-genome sequencing, we identified the transgene insertion site on chromosome 4 approximately 6 kb upstream of Echdc2.
